messages.author: bfa4a88c8a5bc54e
messages.subject: Equivalence of parameterisation for MCMC
parts:
Hello all,

I'm generally interested in playing around with different parameterisations to improve MCMC mixing. I've got a high dimensional model that isn't mixing all that well. Specifically, it's an ordered probit item response model with correlated random individual and correlated random item effects on mu and sigma, with correlated random thresholds as well. So there's three seperate multivariate distributions in this model. I know the non-centered multivariate parameterisation is different from centered. However, I'd like to know, are the following two formulations equivalent in terms of MCMC sampling?

# Random individual effects for each individual i, ..., N
for (i in 1:n) {
   eps[i] ~ dnorm(0, sd = eps.sigma)
   mu[i] <- alpha + eps[i]
   y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], sd = sigma[i])
}

vs.

for (i in 1:n) {
   mu[i] ~ dnorm(alpha, sd = eps.sigma)
   y[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], sd = sigma[i])
}

I'd like to know because if these two formulations are the same, that simplifies the trial and error to see which approach mixes best. For instance, I've found that the centered multivariate thresholds mixes way better than the non-centered, but the non-centered multivariate item effects mix better than the centered. (FYI, I'm aware that the two formulations above aren't centered vs. non-centered but just two ways of writing the centered form.)

Thanks for reading!

Matt

messages.author: 0e6210fc31f1213e
messages.subject: Re: Equivalence of parameterisation for MCMC
parts:
Hi Matthijs,
I suppose there is a prior on the alpha ?
If that is the case (as I suppose), then in terms of sampling both formulation are slightly different.
In the top one, each sampling of alpha triggers the update of all mu[i], and the evaluation of a density ratio (not sure of the statistical term for that) of all y[i] (as all mu[i] were modified)
In the bottom one, each sampling of alpha triggers the evaluation of all density ratio mu[i].

Given that, I think the top one would be slower but alpha would mix better, while the bottom one would be faster but alpha mixing would be worse.
If dimension is really high the top one should be too slow compared to the bottom one, but that is just a guess.

(This is just based on my knowledge on MCMC sampling though, I have no experience with this kind of model)
Hope this helps (and good luck !)
Rémi

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Equivalence of parameterisation for MCMC
parts:
Hi Matthijs,

As you more or less have worked through by computational experiment, the mixing does differ, and it is problem-specific.  Here is a paper on that point: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1198/jcgs.2011.203main.

It has been an idea to implement a strategy like this automatically in nimble, although it would take some careful model inspection and processing of relationships.  If you or anyone is interested, please say so!

HTH!
Perry
